questions.enonce_markdown: Outline the sequence of events that occur during the formation of a nerve impulse. *[9 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
A nerve impulse is a wave of **depolarisation (an action potential)** travelling along the axon membrane. It forms as follows.

**1. Resting potential (axon at rest)**
The **sodium-potassium pump** uses ATP to pump **3 $\mathrm{Na^+}$ out and 2 $\mathrm{K^+}$ in**. The membrane is much more permeable to $\mathrm{K^+}$ (through open leak channels) than to $\mathrm{Na^+}$, so $\mathrm{K^+}$ diffuses out. Large negatively charged proteins stay inside. The outside is therefore positive relative to the inside: the membrane is **polarised** with a **resting potential of about $-70$ mV**.

**2. Stimulus and depolarisation**
A stimulus (electrical, chemical, mechanical) makes some **voltage-gated $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels** open. If the membrane potential reaches the **threshold (about $-55$ mV)**, many more $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels open (positive feedback) and $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ions **rush in** by facilitated diffusion. The inside becomes positive, reaching about **$+40$ mV**: **depolarisation**.

**3. Repolarisation**
At the peak the $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels close (and are inactivated) and **voltage-gated $\mathrm{K^+}$ channels open**. $\mathrm{K^+}$ ions diffuse **out**, so the inside becomes negative again: **repolarisation**. The $\mathrm{K^+}$ channels close slowly, so the potential briefly falls below the resting value (**hyperpolarisation**, about $-80$ mV).

**4. Recovery**
The sodium-potassium pump and the leak channels restore the **resting ion distribution** and the resting potential. During the **refractory period** (while the $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels are inactivated) the membrane cannot respond to a new stimulus, so impulses are **separate** and travel in **one direction** only.

**5. Propagation**
Local currents flow between the depolarised region and the next resting region, bringing it to threshold, so the action potential moves along the axon. It follows the **all-or-nothing law** (it either occurs fully or not at all; the size does not depend on the strength of the stimulus). In **myelinated** neurones the impulse jumps from one **node of Ranvier** to the next (**saltatory conduction**), which is much faster.

**Diagram expected.** Draw a graph of membrane potential (mV, from $-80$ to $+40$) against time (ms, 0 to about 5). Label the resting potential ($-70$ mV), threshold ($-55$ mV), depolarisation ($\mathrm{Na^+}$ in), peak ($+40$ mV), repolarisation ($\mathrm{K^+}$ out), hyperpolarisation, and return to resting potential.

questions.enonce_markdown: How are impulses transmitted from one neurone to another? *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Impulses pass from one neurone to the next across a **synapse**: the **presynaptic knob** of one neurone is separated from the **postsynaptic membrane** of the next by a gap of about **20 nm (the synaptic cleft)**. Transmission is **chemical**, by a **neurotransmitter** (for example **acetylcholine**).

1. The action potential arrives at the **presynaptic knob** and **depolarises** its membrane.
2. **Voltage-gated calcium channels open** and $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ions **enter** the knob.
3. The $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ makes **synaptic vesicles** (containing acetylcholine) move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing the transmitter into the cleft by **exocytosis**.
4. Acetylcholine **diffuses across the cleft** and binds to **specific receptor proteins** on the postsynaptic membrane.
5. This opens **ligand-gated $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels**; $\mathrm{Na^+}$ enters and the postsynaptic membrane is depolarised (an **excitatory postsynaptic potential**). If summation brings it to threshold, a **new action potential** starts in the second neurone.
6. The transmitter is quickly removed: the enzyme **acetylcholinesterase** hydrolyses acetylcholine to **choline and ethanoic acid**, which are taken back into the presynaptic knob and used (with ATP from the many mitochondria) to **make acetylcholine again**. This stops continuous stimulation of the second neurone.

**Notes.** Because only the presynaptic knob contains vesicles and only the postsynaptic membrane has receptors, transmission is **unidirectional**. Some transmitters (e.g. GABA) are **inhibitory**: they open $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ channels and hyperpolarise the postsynaptic membrane, making an impulse less likely.

**Diagram expected.** A labelled synapse: presynaptic knob with mitochondria, vesicles and $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ channels, synaptic cleft with transmitter molecules, postsynaptic membrane with receptors, and arrows showing the direction of the impulse.

questions.enonce_markdown: Briefly explain how the hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland in coordination. *[4 marks]* *(9, 7, 4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **hypothalamus** is the part of the brain that links the nervous system and the hormonal system. It controls the **pituitary gland** (hanging below it) in two ways.

**1. Control of the posterior pituitary (by nerve cells)**
Special **neurosecretory cells** have their cell bodies in the hypothalamus. They make the hormones **ADH (antidiuretic hormone) and oxytocin**, which pass **down their axons** to the posterior lobe, where they are stored in the nerve endings. When the hypothalamus receives information (for example **osmoreceptors** detect a high blood osmotic pressure) the neurones send **nerve impulses** and the hormone is **released into the blood**.

**2. Control of the anterior pituitary (by releasing hormones)**
Neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus secrete **releasing hormones and inhibiting hormones** (e.g. TRH, CRH, GnRH, growth-hormone-releasing hormone) into a **portal system** of blood capillaries that runs directly to the anterior lobe. These **stimulate or inhibit** the anterior pituitary to secrete its hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, growth hormone, prolactin). These in turn control other glands.

**Feedback.** When the level of a hormone from the target gland (e.g. thyroxine, cortisol, sex hormones) rises, it acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary to reduce release of the releasing hormone (**negative feedback**), so that hormone levels are kept stable.
